## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m1-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Linear program</dt><dd>Decisions (outputs, flows), a goal (lowest running cost) and rules (balance, sizes, ramp, network), all linear.</dd>
<dt>Dual of a balance row</dt><dd>The extra cost per MWh of a small change in that row's demand: the price at that bus and hour. At a corner of the model the step up and the step down differ.</dd>
<dt>Ramp prices</dt><dd>A slow plant links hours and produces $0 and $80 prices; the $80 matches no plant's offer.</dd>
<dt>DC power flow</dt><dd>Power splits over every path by the lines' reactance: two thirds on the direct line of an equal triangle.</dd>
<dt>Congestion</dt><dd>A full line splits one price into locational prices. Loads then pay more than generators are paid; the difference is the congestion rent, $13,200 at noon with the line at 110 MW.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Prices from PTDFs, and where the congestion money goes</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Take Prairie Town as the reference bus. A power transfer distribution factor $\text{PTDF}_{\ell n}$ is the share of 1 MW injected at bus $n$, and taken out in town, that flows on line $\ell$. In an equal triangle, an injection at the Ridge puts $2/3$ on Ridge–Town and $1/3$ on the path through the Gas Hub. In a lossless DC model, with $\mu_\ell$ the value of 1 MW more limit on line $\ell$ in that hour:

$$\text{LMP}_n = \text{LMP}_\text{Town} - \sum_\ell \text{PTDF}_{\ell n}\,\mu_\ell .$$

At noon with the line at 110 MW, $\mu = \$120$: the Ridge gets $80 - \tfrac{2}{3} \times 120 = \$0$ and the Gas Hub $80 - \tfrac{1}{3} \times 120 = \$40$.

Congestion rent is what loads pay minus what generators are paid, each at its own bus's price:

| Noon, line at 110 MW | \$ in the hour |
|---|---|
| Loads pay: 311 MWh × \$80 | \$24,880 |
| Nuclear plant, in town: 100 MWh × \$80 | \$8,000 |
| Gas Hub: 92 MWh × \$40 | \$3,680 |
| Wind Ridge: 119 MWh × \$0 | \$0 |
| Congestion rent: loads minus generators | \$13,200 for the hour |

In this DC model the rent also equals each full line's $\mu$ times its flow, $120 \times 110$ MW. It is not the price gap between the line's two ends times its flow ($80 \times 110 = \$8{,}800$).

Many organized markets use congestion revenue to fund financial transmission rights, under their own settlement and funding rules. Their prices also add a third part for losses, which a DC model leaves out ([FERC Energy Primer](https://www.ferc.gov/sites/default/files/2020-06/energy-primer-2020_0.pdf), p. 64).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>When a price is not unique</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A dual is a slope. At a corner of the model the slope differs on each side, so check both sides. At 14:00 with the line at 110 MW, the gas combined-cycle plant runs at exactly its size, 150 MW:

| In town at 14:00 | Per MWh |
|---|---|
| Step up: one more MWh needs the peaker | costs \$200 |
| Step down: one MWh less | saves only \$80 |
| The solver's dual | \$80, one end of that range |

If the two sides differ, say which side your question is about. A mixed-integer solve ([M2](m02-unit-commitment.html)) does not provide these LP shadow prices; after fixing its on/off decisions, a dispatch LP gives prices conditional on them.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this model leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Losses, voltage magnitudes and reactive power: a DC model uses only voltage-angle differences, holds voltage magnitudes fixed and is lossless. A17 (upcoming) runs a small AC power flow to show when that matters.</li>
<li>Outages: real dispatch keeps flows safe if any one line or plant fails (the N-1 rule).</li>
<li>Start-ups and minimum run times: those need on/off decisions, a mixed-integer program (<a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>).</li>
<li>Offers and price-responsive demand: here costs stand in for offers, and demand is fixed.</li>
<li>Size: real markets price thousands of locations; the algebra is the same.</li>
</ul>
<p>Modeler's note: <a href="m03-capacity-expansion.html">M3</a> adds investment decisions to this model, and the Modeler checkpoint <a href="ck-m-unseen-problem.html">CK-M</a> asks you to formulate, solve and verify a model you have not seen. The Researcher studio <a href="r05-build-validate.html">R5</a> makes verification and validation a routine.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m1-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="offer" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A bus price always equals the offer of some plant.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At noon the town's $80 matches no offer: it is 2 × $40 − 1 × $0, set by the full line's physics.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="ridge" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “When the line out of a wind area is full, the price at the wind farm can fall to zero.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Wind Ridge spills power it cannot send, so one more MWh there is free: its price is $0.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="market" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The dual of a balance row is the price a real market must charge.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It is a marginal value under this model's assumptions: fixed plants, costs as offers, no losses, this network and day. Markets clear real offers under many more rules.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m1">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mu" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">At noon the full Ridge–Town line (110 MW) has μ = $120. If its limit rose to 111 MW for the noon interval only, the day's running cost would…</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">fall by $120</li><li data-value="b">fall by $80</li><li data-value="c">fall by $40</li><li data-value="d">not change</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fall by $120. Swapping 1 MW of Gas Hub output for Ridge output adds only 2/3 − 1/3 = 1/3 MW to this line, so 1 MW more room lets 3 MW of free Ridge power replace 3 MW of $40 gas.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="back" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">Which change brings the three noon prices back together?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Add 50 MW of solar on Wind Ridge</li><li data-value="b">Raise the Ridge–Town limit to 140 MW</li><li data-value="c">Raise the gas price</li><li data-value="d">Lower the town's demand by 1 MW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Raise the limit to 140 MW: at noon the line then needs only 134 MW, so it has room and one price returns. More Ridge solar would only add to the spill.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
